evidence.claim: Kishida said wage increases were central to a virtuous cycle of growth and distribution, called for a tax system that promotes wage increases, urged environments where SMEs can pass through raw-material cost increases, sought a minimum wage above 1,000 yen, and pledged more human-capital investment and better disclosure of non-financial information.
evidence.title: Policy Speech by Prime Minister KISHIDA Fumio to the 208th Session of the Diet
evidence.excerpt: Kishida said wage increases were central to a virtuous cycle of growth and distribution, called for a tax system that promotes wage increases, urged environments where SMEs can pass through raw-material cost increases, sought a minimum wage above 1,000 yen, and pledged more human-capital investment and better disclosure of non-financial information.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official Diet policy speech with detailed economic measures.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Kishida policy program and distribution strategy.
contrary_evidence: The speech sets direction but does not itself show the economy responded as intended.

evidence.claim: Kishida said the 'Grand Design and Action Plan for a New Form of Capitalism' would turn social issues the market could not solve into new growth sources, with concrete multi-year plans for startups, green transformation, and asset-income expansion, and that Japan would then move to implementation after the election.
evidence.title: Joint Meeting of the Council on Economic and Fiscal Policy and the Council of New Form of Capitalism Realization
evidence.excerpt: Kishida said the 'Grand Design and Action Plan for a New Form of Capitalism' would turn social issues the market could not solve into new growth sources, with concrete multi-year plans for startups, green transformation, and asset-income expansion, and that Japan would then move to implementation after the election.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official PM action record capturing the policy package and timing.
contrary_evidence: The document is a plan-to-action transition, not proof of realized economic gains yet.

evidence.claim: Kishida said further investment in people was needed to realize a new form of capitalism, calling for development of highly professional human resources, internationalized education, support for universities, learning support, and recurrent education under government-wide implementation.
evidence.title: Council for the Creation of Future Education
evidence.excerpt: Kishida said further investment in people was needed to realize a new form of capitalism, calling for development of highly professional human resources, internationalized education, support for universities, learning support, and recurrent education under government-wide implementation.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official prime-minister action record with detailed human-capital agenda.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Kishida leadership over productivity and education policy.
contrary_evidence: This is still a reform agenda rather than a measured output.

evidence.claim: Kishida held the Council of New Form of Capitalism Realization to discuss a draft comprehensive economic package and reinforcements for passing on costs and supporting SMEs in response to wage and minimum-wage increases.
evidence.title: Council of New Form of Capitalism Realization
evidence.excerpt: Kishida held the Council of New Form of Capitalism Realization to discuss a draft comprehensive economic package and reinforcements for passing on costs and supporting SMEs in response to wage and minimum-wage increases.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official PM action note on the policy-development meeting.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Kishida leadership over SME and price-pass-through policy.
contrary_evidence: It is still a planning document, not an implementation result.

evidence.claim: Japanese top firms offered pay rises of more than 2 percent at annual wage talks, still short of Kishida's request for 3 percent or more, and analysts said the increase was too small to deliver a big economic boost.
evidence.title: Japan Inc hikes pay by more than 2%, not enough for a big economic boost
evidence.excerpt: Japanese top firms offered pay rises of more than 2 percent at annual wage talks, still short of Kishida's request for 3 percent or more, and analysts said the increase was too small to deliver a big economic boost.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous Reuters reporting on wage outcomes and their policy significance.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Indirectly tied to Kishida's wage-growth agenda; firms determined the final pay offers.
contrary_evidence: The article itself says the increase was insufficient to boost the economy materially.

evidence.claim: Japan's average minimum wage was approved to rise by 31 yen, or a record 3.3 percent, to 961 yen per hour, and Reuters reported that Kishida was counting on the increase to distribute wealth more broadly and support a sustainable recovery path.
evidence.title: Japan's planned record minimum wage hike opens path to sustained GDP growth
evidence.excerpt: Japan's average minimum wage was approved to rise by 31 yen, or a record 3.3 percent, to 961 yen per hour, and Reuters reported that Kishida was counting on the increase to distribute wealth more broadly and support a sustainable recovery path.
evidence.source_locator: Opening paragraphs and lines 424-426 in the open text
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous Reuters reporting on an official wage decision and its political meaning.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly aligned with Kishida's wage-growth agenda, though the formal decision process is ministry-led.
contrary_evidence: A minimum-wage hike helps distribution, but by itself it does not prove durable broad prosperity.

evidence.claim: Kishida said the Cabinet approved a roughly 72 trillion yen economic package with 39 trillion yen of fiscal spending, intended to raise GDP by 4.6 percent, reduce consumer prices by more than 1.2 percent through 2023, lower electricity fees by 20 percent, provide average households 45,000 yen of aid, support SMEs, tourism, and a 1 trillion yen human-investment package over five years.
evidence.title: Press Conference by Prime Minister Kishida
evidence.excerpt: Kishida said the Cabinet approved a roughly 72 trillion yen economic package with 39 trillion yen of fiscal spending, intended to raise GDP by 4.6 percent, reduce consumer prices by more than 1.2 percent through 2023, lower electricity fees by 20 percent, provide average households 45,000 yen of aid, support SMEs, tourism, and a 1 trillion yen human-investment package over five years.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official PM transcript with precise package scale and intended effects.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Kishida fiscal-policy decision and implementation design.
contrary_evidence: The package relies heavily on subsidies and projections; it does not by itself prove durable productivity gains.

evidence.claim: Kishida said the government would provide the average household with 47,000 yen of assistance, continue business support for electricity and gas bills, and expand child-related assistance including 100,000 yen in flexible support and a record increase in the childbirth lump-sum allowance to 500,000 yen.
evidence.title: Press Conference by Prime Minister Kishida
evidence.excerpt: Kishida said the government would provide the average household with 47,000 yen of assistance, continue business support for electricity and gas bills, and expand child-related assistance including 100,000 yen in flexible support and a record increase in the childbirth lump-sum allowance to 500,000 yen.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official year-end PM transcript with concrete household and child-support amounts.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Kishida distributive policy and family-support decision.
contrary_evidence: This is relief spending, not proof of durable broad prosperity or real wage gains.

evidence.claim: Kishida said the ruling parties had agreed on a tax reform proposal including a new corporate surtax of 4.0 to 4.5 percent with exemptions for roughly 24 million yen of converted earnings for SMEs, while not increasing the income-tax burden and securing stable revenue.
evidence.title: Press Conference by Prime Minister Kishida
evidence.excerpt: Kishida said the ruling parties had agreed on a tax reform proposal including a new corporate surtax of 4.0 to 4.5 percent with exemptions for roughly 24 million yen of converted earnings for SMEs, while not increasing the income-tax burden and securing stable revenue.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official PM transcript on the year-end tax package with explicit rate and exemption details.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Kishida fiscal-policy and distribution choice.
contrary_evidence: It shifts the burden toward business profits and still does not guarantee stronger household purchasing power.

evidence.claim: Japan's core consumer inflation accelerated to a 40-year high in October, reaching 3.6 percent year on year, driven by currency weakness and imported cost pressures while the Bank of Japan kept policy ultra-easy.
evidence.title: Japan's inflation hits 40-year high as BOJ sticks to easy policy
evidence.excerpt: Japan's core consumer inflation accelerated to a 40-year high in October, reaching 3.6 percent year on year, driven by currency weakness and imported cost pressures while the Bank of Japan kept policy ultra-easy.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous Reuters reporting on a major macro shock and central-bank response.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mostly macro context outside Kishida's direct control, though it framed his fiscal intervention.
contrary_evidence: This is largely external-cost inflation, not a direct signal of Kishida mismanagement by itself.

evidence.claim: Reuters reported that Kishida had stepped up his call for better pay as a weak yen and higher commodity prices pushed inflation up, and that the 2023 spring wage round was the biggest in about 30 years, highlighting how the 2022 wage environment had lagged prices.
evidence.title: Japan's workers get biggest pay rises in decades as inflation surges
evidence.excerpt: Reuters reported that Kishida had stepped up his call for better pay as a weak yen and higher commodity prices pushed inflation up, and that the 2023 spring wage round was the biggest in about 30 years, highlighting how the 2022 wage environment had lagged prices.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters retrospective linking Kishida's wage agenda to the inflation environment and later wage gains.
evidence.period_fit: Retrospective context on the 2022 wage trajectory
evidence.ruler_attribution: Indirect; useful mainly for the trajectory from Kishida's 2022 agenda to later wage results.
contrary_evidence: It is retrospective and partly outside the target year, so it should be used cautiously.

evidence.claim: The IMF said Japan was recovering with strong policy support, but higher commodity prices and the Ukraine conflict would slow domestic demand; it also urged gradual rebuilding of fiscal buffers and structural reforms to lift potential growth.
evidence.title: Japan: 2022 Article IV Consultation-Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Japan
evidence.excerpt: The IMF said Japan was recovering with strong policy support, but higher commodity prices and the Ukraine conflict would slow domestic demand; it also urged gradual rebuilding of fiscal buffers and structural reforms to lift potential growth.
evidence.source_locator: Summary and policy recommendations in the report page
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Authoritative IMF country report with explicit policy advice and constraints.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mostly baseline and policy recommendation context rather than a direct Kishida action record.
contrary_evidence: This is advisory and does not demonstrate that Kishida carried out the recommended reforms.

evidence.claim: The ministry said real wages fell 0.9 percent in 2022 because nominal wages rose 2.1 percent while the consumer-price index rose 3.0 percent, and it linked the policy response to continued wage increases and a 1 trillion yen human-investment package.
evidence.title: 加藤大臣会見概要 ｜令和５年２月７日｜大臣記者会見
evidence.publisher: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare
evidence.excerpt: The ministry said real wages fell 0.9 percent in 2022 because nominal wages rose 2.1 percent while the consumer-price index rose 3.0 percent, and it linked the policy response to continued wage increases and a 1 trillion yen human-investment package.
evidence.source_locator: Reporter Q&A and minister answer in the open page
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official ministry statement reporting the annual outcome and policy response.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Outcome under Kishida's term, but only partly under his direct control because prices and wage bargaining were external and decentralized.
contrary_evidence: Real wages falling is a direct negative on household prosperity, even if policy was trying to reverse it.

unresolved_gaps: Stronger direct evidence of Kishida's personal control over police, prosecutors, and protective institutions before and after the Abe assassination.
More evidence that the church-scandal and protest responses reduced actual harm rather than only improving the public narrative.
More independent evidence that the 2022 growth/distribution package actually changed household welfare or investment outcomes rather than only announcing them.
Better separation of Kishida's policy effect from BOJ policy, exchange-rate moves, and imported inflation shocks.
Direct year-end outcome evidence for child, fertility, and social-service gains attributable to the 2022 package.
More subgroup evidence on single-parent households, disabled people, housing insecurity, and food insecurity.
Direct, traceable evidence of Kishida's own assets, private interests, donor links, or personal self-enrichment is missing.
Independent corroboration of the personal claim that Kishida had no links to the former Unification Church and that his vetting instructions were fully followed.
More independent evidence on whether the 2022 startup, digital, and green-growth agenda actually produced measurable execution, not just planning.
Clearer separation of Kishida's own execution from external shocks and inherited macro conditions when judging the economic package and wage trajectory.
